item.title: Make the Hedonic Treadmill a Place You Want to Be
item.description:
Hedonic Treadmill

Make the Hedonic Treadmill a Place You Want to Be

To escape the grind, try less social comparison and more self-actualisation.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • The hedonic treadmill brings us back to baseline mood over time and makes it hard to be fully satisfied.
  • This pattern is unavoidable, so work with the treadmill without accelerating its immiserating dynamics.
  • Self-actualisation can overcome the treadmill by generating pleasant, fulfilling, and valuable experiences.
  • This requires harmonising your emotions, motivations, values, and reasons.

Do you “just want to be happy,” but feel like something is always missing?

Do you feel like you’re sprinting towards a rest that never arrives?

Do your highs never last as long as you’d like?

You might be stuck on what psychologists call the hedonic treadmill.

The hedonic treadmill: working hard to stay in the same place.
Source: Céline Cao/Unsplash

There are two bits to the treadmill. The first is homeostatically protected mood. Our high-arousal states, whether positive (joy) or negative (sadness), tend not to last. We return in short order to a mildly positive, low-arousal state.

The second is always being able to see ways that life could be better. For example, in our research interviewing people about how they report their life satisfaction, many say they would never give more than 8/10 because they wouldn’t want to say that they are completely satisfied.

One respondent who was 8/10 said: “If I’m really honest, I think ‘what could make my life better?’ I don’t actually know. I really have no clue.”

But they were still adamantly 8/10.

The hedonic treadmill has evolution’s fingerprints all over it. If we were always ecstatic or depressed, we wouldn’t prepare for the winter so industriously. If we weren’t on the lookout for ways to make things better, we’d eventually be overwhelmed by parasites and predators or outcompeted by rival tribes.

Why fear the treadmill?

Historically, we invented social technologies for dampening the effects of the hedonic treadmill. For example, most religions have gratitude practices that make us mindful of the good things we already have, like mealtime prayers.

Prayers of gratitude at meals can keep us focused on the great things we already have.
Source: Cemrecan Yurtman/Unsplash

Recently, though, the materialistic, competitive, and hierarchical culture of capitalism has encouraged us to lean into the treadmill. You could always have a fancier car, or a further promotion at work.

This makes us miserable. As the adage goes, and as scientific research shows, “comparison is the thief of joy.”

People exhausted by the treadmill have recently revived many ancient techniques for getting off it. Buddhism argues that desire is the root of all suffering and teaches charitable giving as a way to quieten the desire for more. The Stoics advise mindful attention to present experiences, as Marcus Aurelius writes: “each day provides its own gifts.” Epicurus counsels us to take joy in what we have already achieved: “Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not; remember that what you now have was once among the things you only hoped for.”

Such insights should form a core part of your well-being practice, but in my book Beyond Happy I suggest a different overarching paradigm: Make the treadmill a place you want to be.

The treadmill is biological reality. Gratitude and related techniques can help you slow down and notice life’s delights, but you can’t stand still.

So you need to organize your life so that its dynamism isn’t nauseating and it continuously generates pleasant, fulfilling, and valuable experiences.

You’re not trying to get ahead, but you enjoy moving.

This dynamic cuts out the relentlessness of the treadmill and keeps you focused on what’s good in your life. There’s no attention left over for dissatisfaction. It also generates new experiences so that you’re regularly up from the homeostatic baseline. With a bit of training in how to savour positive moods, you’ll reverse the misery vortex of the treadmill into a good-life vortex.

How to escape the grind

So how do you do this? The short answer is self-actualization.

You need to learn to listen to your emotions, understand your values, be extremely mindful of your motivations, and articulate the reasons why you live the life you do.

You then need to make all that coherent and internally consistent. This is a long and iterative process of refinement that I call the coalescence of being. Coalescence begins by turning inward. You cannot identify your intrinsic motivations or ground your values in what makes you indignant or gives you a warm and fuzzy feeling without first gaining some distance from the social influences conditioning you in their preferred direction.

Turn inwards: The best guide to your self-actualisation is you.
Source: Vince Fleming/Unsplash

After self-discovery comes self-creation. You need to experiment with the identity that inspires you and see if it’s a good fit. Introspecting on the emotional and social feedback you get along the way will help you make refinements and recalibrations. You might love ballet, for example, but after a few years in the community you find you much prefer making the costumes to dancing.

The final stage is turning outwards to find your tribe. Well-being is something we do together. Those pleasant, fulfilling, and valuable experiences that make the treadmill a place we want to be often come from other people, or things we achieve with them. It’s rewarding to stitch a tutu, but even more so when we see it worn in a production of Swan Lake, contributing to something meaningful for the whole group.

There are other key techniques for managing the treadmill.

  • Don’t set targets that are essentially limitless or subject to very strong comparison effects, like “getting rich.” Focus instead on qualitative goals, like the strength of your relationships and the success of community projects.

  • Don’t confuse self-actualization with self-optimization. Growth is about becoming our full self, not our most competitive or optimized self.

  • For some people, like professional athletes, winning is an authentic need. But for most of us, a fixation on being “better” just accelerates the treadmill or puts it on an incline. A balanced life working on shared goals will provide more opportunities for pleasure, fulfilment, and purpose.

  • Finally, stay mindful. It’s easy to slip back into trying to outpace the treadmill if you don’t pay attention to all the great things that are already happening every week.

item.title: Using Peripheral Vision to Unleash New Perspectives
item.description:
Self-Help

Using Peripheral Vision to Unleash New Perspectives

Widening your lens can make a difference in your relational well-being.

Posted October 31, 2026

Key points
  • Broader perception helps break free from rigid, stress-inducing models of certainty.
  • Using a stereoscopic lens to zoom in and out can help resolve conflict.
  • A peripheral visualiztion excericise offers an improvisational means to make a difference in your life.

“The moon commends herself to the matter-of-fact people by her usefulness, and makes her uselessness adored by poets, artists, and all lovers in all lands.” —Walt Whitman

"Sometimes change is directly visible, but sometimes it is apparent only to peripheral vision, altering the meaning of the foreground.” —Mary Catherine Bateson

I wonder at times what is necessary and what is not. Water is, but is it, when you cup your hands to drink, encompassing many yin-and-yang contexts? Maneuvering life's many different manifestations is not always easy. Richard Adams, in his book Watership Down, echoing Walt Whitman's quote above, once said, "We need daylight, and to that extent it is utilitarian, but moonlight we do not need.” Maybe so or not, depending on one's perspective.

Source: Natasha Rabin (c) with permission

During my 40-plus years as a systemic psychotherapist, the most effective visual exercise that I use to help set a productive framework for therapy is peripheral vision. It is a powerful segue into recognizing how one can expand and improve perspective in an aesthetic manner. It helps us reveal how each relational experience offers a multitude of possible contexts, all of which are simultaneously part of other wider contexts. This interactional reality, familiar to all artists, stems from how William Blake could see the world in a mere grain of sand. Peripheral vision offers opportunities that foster improvisational possibilities, which is how our species learns and evolves. All artistic endeavors come to fruition this way, as does nature herself in her messy and beautiful ways. This is systems or ecological thinking at its best. It opens the door to random, creative, novel ways to harmonize and mutually learn from each other and our environment.

Most literature on peripheral vision describes the physical attributes separately from the mental/emotional ones, only hinting at its potential to create a wider, all-inclusive lens to see, celebrate, and take advantage of our shared global interdependency. Given the way our autonomic nervous system works, the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis can and often does get stuck when the sympathetic part of our nervous system is revved up in our fight-or-flight mode. You don't have to save your life 24 hours a day. Peripheral vision may help calm us by giving us more space to see alternatives that can reduce stress.

Andrew Huberman, a neuroscientist at Stanford often quoted on “panoramic vision,” believes it stimulates calmness; however, he warns that it could lead to such focus that it can be used to increase productivity rather than relieve stress.

That is a true cultural constraint, especially in Western cultures. However, in my experience, it also encourages and maintains a pathway back to the parasympathetic, calm part of our nervous system for better decision-making. Mary Catherine Bateson advocated for the wider benefits of peripheral viewing through "recognizing that the self is not identical through time; it is a first step in celebrating it as fluid and variable, shaped and reshaped by learning.” Albert Einstein concurred that important discoveries were made by those willing to leave the details and "take in a bigger picture." Kaja Perina, in a recent Psychology Today Editor's Note regarding the search for the Goldilocks Moment, writes, "You don't always know when you're there, after all. It is our nature to miss fulfillment in the here and now."

When I work with those exploring better relationships and striving to resolve conflicts, I try to help them avoid models that try to fit everything into narrow outcomes of certainty (see my recent blog post about the value of being uncertain). These models just do not get your nervous system unglued with consistency. Our vagus nerve, the most intriguing wandering part of our nervous system, is energized through compassion that relates to your specific needs. According to Dacher Keltner, author of Born to Be Good, it even glows as an aesthetic response to your personal needs. The process recognizes how our ecology of mind and body works in countless ways.

This opens the door to understanding our need to share our individual concerns in a harmonizing, win-win way. It's a biological need that drives first-order change toward individual health and, in turn, influences other related changes. It demonstrates how our whole being has a unique and distinct role in sustaining our relationships.

Here is my induction exercise using peripheral vision for those looking for differences that make changes and impact their lives. It is interwoven, as is the nature of complexity and life, with improvisational possibilities and can be adapted for individuals, couples, and families.

Start by sitting in a comfortable chair in a room with a view of the outside. Begin by doing some “coherent breathing,” developed by Stephen Elliott, to soothe the vagus nerve, the nerve of compassion and security (a six-second inhale and a six-second exhale with a positive thought) for 5 to 10 minutes. Then "will" each muscle area of your body to relax progressively downward, head to toe. With your body relaxed, look straight ahead and imagine a camera-like lens in your eyes with peripheral vision, seeing each wall in your room as well as the ceiling and floor. Pause, look inside yourself, and visualize the differences you would like to see in your life right now.

After a few minutes, zoom outward beyond the immediate room to your outside view. Imagine using all your senses to see how you might make the differences you desire. Now close your eyes and, with your mind's eye, zoom even further outward into your community, pausing and using all your senses to accept whatever arises from your subconscious regarding making a difference that matters in your life. After a few more minutes, with your eyes still closed, zoom further out into the wider world you live in, including contexts such as schooling, medicine, work, media, religion, etc. Again, pause and reflect on the differences you are seeking to create. After a few minutes, zoom back inward to your room, pause, and revisit your original desire, noticing any changes in how you may make that initial difference

In all the hundreds of times I have used this exercise, everyone has had a new, useful perspective that helped them better understand how to proceed in relation to their world and with others.
